blocks.text: The other passage is from Bereshit Rabbah, section 83, and it is no better understood than the former: הביא חכינא וזיוג לה חרדון ויצאת מהם חברבר, He brought a chacina and coupled it with the chardon, and from them was born the chabarber. The subject is Anah, who is read to have found הימים jemim in the desert, that is, to have come upon the Emim, as we have shown elsewhere ^{e)}. But the Hebrews understand mules, of which Anah was supposedly the first inventor, by bringing a she-ass to a horse or a wild ass. Since such a coupling of different species is forbidden by the Law of Moses, God, they say, in punishment for this crime, chose himself also to mix animals of different species, so that something harmful to man would be born from them. So he coupled the חרדון chardon with the חכינה chacina; from these was born a third species, worse than either, namely the חברבר chabarber [col. 1058], whose bite is so harmful that מעולם לא נשך אדם חברבר וחיה, a man whom the chabarber has bitten never recovers. Hence the Jerusalem Talmud, in Berakhot, fol. 12. b.: מימיו לא יאמר לך אדם שעקצו חברבר וחיה שנשכו כלב שיטה וחיה שבעטתו פרדה וחיה No one will ever tell you that he recovered after being stung by a chabarber, or recovered after being bitten by a rabid dog, or recovered after being kicked by a she-mule. And on fol. 9. a. a little story is told of R. Chanina, son of Dosa, who, while he was praying, was bitten by a chabarber and did not stop praying. Yet he himself did not die; rather the chabarber that had bitten him died. And so it was said: אי לו לאדם שנשכו חברבר ואי לו לחברבר שנשך את רבי חנינה Woe to the man whom the chabarber has bitten! But woe to the chabarber that has bitten Rabbi Chanina! Now if you consult the lexicographers to learn what the חרדון chardon is, what the חכינא chacina is, and what the חברבר chabarber is, they will teach you that the chardon is a toad [II, 480] or a tortoise, and the chacina a kind of serpent, and that from their union the chabarber was born, that is, a beast sharing the nature of both. Since this is utterly absurd, why should we not say here with the Poet,
Shall griffins now be mated with horses? — — —
